newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan inflation set to ease but growth subdued.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan inflation set to ease but growth subdued.

text.p: Central Bank of Kenya economist Maurice Kanga forecast a return to single-digit inflation with the arrival of long rains, but analysts said only an increase in real production could bring about an economic boom.
"It will not happen all at once, because we have yet to recover from the drought, but generally overall inflation will remain below 10 percent this year," Kanga said.
The annualised month-on-month inflation rate rose to 16.1 percent in April from 15.6 percent in March and 11.9 percent in February.
The sharp increase was largely due to the failure of the short rains between October and December which brought drought to key growing areas and boosted the prices of staple foods.

Long rains arrived last month, but economists said Kanga's forecast was too optimistic given this is an election year. They said investors suffering from election jitters could defer major investment decisions to next year.
They pointed out last year's growth in gross domestic product (GDP), estimated at 4.6 percent, was below the five percent target. They projected growth this year of six percent.

The country is still haunted by the gross monetary mismanagement seen in last elections five years ago. According to Kanga, the growth in money supply level seen in that one year should have taken six years to achieve with an average GDP growth rate of five percent.
"I cannot visualise the central bank printing any money. Nobody, even the bad guys, wants what happened in 1992 to repeat itself," he added.

The central bank's attempt to contain inflation to single digits by strictly monitoring money supply, analysts said, has also created a vicious cycle where the central bank competes with commercial banks for deposits and pushes interest rates higher.
"The economy is hurting. We are not producing. The central bank is distorting the economy by having everybody invest in short-term paper," said economist Professor Joseph Kimura.

Kenya's economy is 60 percent driven by agriculture. Despite higher coffee and tea prices in the international markets this year, exporters say their earnings are constrained by a strong shilling and the high cost of borrowing.

"Fundamentally, until the shilling is devalued, the strong shilling will continue to hurt exporters. We are simply not able to create more jobs," a senior official from tea exporter Brooke Bond Kenya told Reuters.
Many businessmen say the high cost of financing is like a leech drawing blood from Kenya's economic veins and in the end will retard business development and hit long-term investment.

Central bank figures show credit to manufacturers rose by only 6.3 percent between February 1996 and February 1997, compared to 42.4 percent between April 1995 and April 1996 while credit to exporters decreased by 20.7 percent compared to a decrease of 2.6 percent in the previous period.

"There are a lot of factors working against growth in the economy, like poor infrastructure and the power blackouts that happen often. What the politicians should ensure instead is that people are motivated enough to produce," Kanga said. -- Nairobi newsroom +254 2 330261
